reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The only official adoption measure in this material comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes religious organizations, the latest figure is 15.0%, against a prior period of 13.7%. The survey first asked the question in September 2023, and the Census Bureau suppresses some values. That number describes a broad service-sector bucket rather than congregations specifically, so it should be read as the closest available official proxy, not a count of churches using AI.

What deployment looks like in this sector is described mainly by Gloo, which presents AI as a foundational capability across its platform, aimed at mission effectiveness, preserving relational ministry, and practical value across what it calls the faith and flourishing ecosystem. Gloo describes values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, with an AI Studio that offers API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, selecting a model per request. This site's own curated points describe Gloo as used by thousands of US churches and as a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations, and they frame the practical territory as sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations.

The research layer is dominated by a small set of named organizations. Barna Group, described here as a Christian research organization providing data on faith, culture, and ministry, is credited in this site's points with the State of the Church work that quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders, and its page material promotes The State of Pastors, Volume 2, along with findings on why young adults attend church. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research is cited for a 45 year history of accurate research on churches and congregational life, and this site's points say it regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption. Pew Research Center's religion work is cited for measuring how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces, though the harvested page material itself covers religious hostility and demographics rather than AI.

The ethics conversation is organized by AI and Faith, which describes itself as a global, pluralist network of faith leaders, scholars, technologists, ethicists, and educators working under five strategic pillars, and which argues that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom to guide AI development. It notes that 85 percent of the world's population claim a religious affiliation, which is the frame for its claim that these issues are spiritual as well as moral. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, is described as convening a multidisciplinary community and promoting research and policy leadership in artificial intelligence and other technology ethics, with practical models for ethical design, development, and deployment. The Notre Dame material also quotes Sullivan saying many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement, and names Lily Abadal, a partner at Catholic school consultants Partners in Mission and a faculty fellow with a Notre Dame project called DELTA, on how AI awareness has been evolving.

On risk and regulation, these sources say relatively little. The Pew material harvested here concerns social hostilities involving religion, reporting that 55 countries had high or very high levels in 2023, up from 45 the previous year, and that restrictions on religion have been tracked across 198 countries and territories since 2007. That is a religious freedom frame, not an AI regulatory frame, and nothing in this material documents rules aimed at AI use by congregations. The risk themes that do appear are ethical and pastoral: the concern about displacement voiced at Notre Dame, and the sector's stated interest in AI that reflects religious values rather than generic commercial defaults.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaway is that the measurement base is thin and borrowed. The Census Bureau figure covers a service-sector category, not churches, and the sector's own evidence comes from Barna, Gloo, and the Hartford Institute rather than from a dedicated official survey. The vendors and platforms that matter here are few and explicitly positioned around values alignment, and the ethical guidance is being written by networks like AI and Faith and academic centers like Notre Dame rather than by regulators. Where the sources are silent, particularly on cost, return on investment, and formal compliance obligations, this material offers nothing to fill the gap.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The University of Notre Dame’s Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to address pressing ethical issues, including artificial intelligence and other technology ethics. The institute states that it engages stakeholders to examine real-world challenges and provide practical models for ethical technology design, development, and deployment. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher, reports that many AI industry workers speak casually about job displacement and the prospect of faster, cheaper work, with some hoping to move beyond work entirely toward family time and hobbies. Lily Abadal, a partner at Partners in Mission and professor at the University of South Florida, notes that awareness of AI has been evolving; she is also a faculty fellow with Notre Dame’s DELTA project on human formation in the age of AI.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group presents itself as a Christian research organization offering data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry. The page advertises a free webcast replay that examines six trends affecting pastoral leadership, drawing on findings from its report *The State of Pastors, Volume 2*. It also promotes a podcast in which pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discuss challenges and opportunities in church leadership. Additionally, Barna reports new data on the social motivators behind why young adults attend church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind, organised under five strategic pillars. It argues that these issues are at root deeply moral, and that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation they are also deeply spiritual, so the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide AI's development and use. The organisation says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around artificial intelligence and related technologies. It quotes a statement that its goal is to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, calling the project deeply humanistic and one that draws on faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions. The page also invites tax-deductible donations and signups to a monthly newsletter.
